context_blurb:
Rain that lands on a hill runs into creeks, soaks into the ground or waits in a marsh, and at last it reaches a lake or the sea. Whatever it washes off the land, from soil to fertiliser, rides along downstream.

A watershed is all the land that drains to one outlet, such as a bay. Nearness does not decide which watershed a place is in; the water's path does. The Susquehanna River rises in New York hills far closer to Lake Ontario, yet it flows south into the Chesapeake Bay. So a farm there whose creeks drain to that river lies in the bay's watershed.

A watershed's edge is its divide, the high ground where rain parts, flowing to this river on one side and the next on the other. Rivers and creeks run through the low middle, so in rugged land the edge mostly follows the tops of ridges and hills.

Groundwater is no hidden lake or river: it fills the pores, tiny spaces between grains, and cracks in rock, like water in a sponge. Below the water table, every pore is full. Porosity is how much of a layer is open space, and permeability is how easily water flows through it. Clay is more than half space, but its pores are so tiny and poorly linked that water barely moves. Gravel holds less water, yet its large, joined spaces let water flow easily, so a well in gravel refills fast. Silt passes water slowly, and solid granite only through cracks.

Pumping a well draws the water table down around it in a funnel-shaped dip called a cone of depression, deepest at the pump. A big well's cone can reach a shallow well nearby and drop the water table below its bottom, so the shallow well runs dry, though deeper ground stays soaked.

Water in the pores helps hold up the ground above, so when it is pumped out, the weight packs the grains tighter. Clay squeezes far more than sand or gravel, so clay layers thin and the land sinks, mostly for good. After decades of pumping for crops, parts of California's San Joaquin Valley had dropped some eight and a half metres by 1970.

A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up storm water and letting it out slowly, which keeps floods downstream lower. Drain and plough it, and the next storm's rain reaches the river much sooner, so the river rises higher and faster. Wetlands along the Mississippi once held at least sixty days of its floodwater; with most drained or filled, they hold about twelve.

Behind a dam the river slows into a still lake, a reservoir, where the sand and mud it carries, called sediment, sink to the lake bed. Big reservoirs trap most of what flows in: Lake Nasser, behind Egypt's Aswan High Dam, holds back over 95 percent of the Nile's. With little new sand to replace what waves carry off, beaches and deltas wear away; the Nile delta has retreated faster since the dam's completion in 1970.

Each summer, where the Mississippi meets the sea, a dead zone forms: bottom water so short of oxygen that most fish flee or die. Fertiliser washed off farms across the river's vast watershed feeds algae; when the algae die and sink, the bacteria rotting them use up the deep water's oxygen. A wet spring washes more fertiliser down the swollen river, so the dead zone grows larger. Extra water does not thin the fertiliser out: the rainy spring of 2019 brought a large dead zone, and the 2012 drought one of the smallest on record.

Winds and Earth's spin drive currents that slowly circle each great ocean in vast loops called gyres, and floating rubbish drifts into a loop's calm middle and stays. So the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, about halfway between Hawaii and California, gathers litter from Pacific shores and nets lost by fishing boats far out at sea. Tides cannot gather it, for they happen across the whole ocean and only slosh water back and forth.

A fish population is overfished when fishing takes fish faster than breeding replaces them. Sardines breed within about a year, so young fish soon fill the gaps. The deep-sea orange roughy breeds only after twenty years or more; one caught at fifteen never bred at all. So with the same share caught each year, the late-breeding orange roughy shrinks far faster; many of its stocks crashed within three to twenty years of fishing.
